items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Names like `pending`, `errors` and `worker` say what they are. The docstring explains the lazy start, cancellation and error behaviour, and an inline comment explains the cleanup-on-cancel loop. Formatting is consistent.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The function is short (about 55 lines) with no dead code. But it rebuilds structured cancellation by hand (`while True: try: await asyncio.gather(...) except CancelledError: ... w.cancel()`) instead of using `asyncio.TaskGroup` as the conventions ask, which makes it harder to change later.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It validates `max_concurrent < 1` and awaits cleanup even if cancelled again. However, `errors.append(exc)` collects every failure and only `raise errors[0]` comes out, so later task exceptions are silently dropped. It also uses a broad `except BaseException`.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: An empty list returns promptly and `ValueError` is raised for `max_concurrent < 1`. But when a task fails, the other tasks are not cancelled and queued tasks still start; the first error is only raised after all tasks finish. This is a documented choice and nothing hangs or leaks.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: The signature and annotations match exactly. Each callable is invoked lazily inside a worker only when a slot is free, and at most once via the shared iterator. It uses only the standard library and has no import-time side effects.
